idiom_name: std::visit(overload{...}, a, b) over two std::variant operands
implementation_notes: For a closed set of types the standard library supplies the whole mechanism: hold both operands as std::variant and call std::visit with a callable that covers every alternative of every variant; the implementation reads each discriminant once and dispatches through a compiler-generated table, so a missing (A,B) case is a compile error rather than a runtime fallback. This replaces the classic accept/visit pair completely - no base class, no accept methods, no vtables, no dynamic allocation. Reach for the classic two-virtual-call visitor (see the classic-visitor variant) when either hierarchy is open, extended elsewhere or crossing an ABI boundary, because std::variant fixes every alternative at compile time.
pitfalls: The overload set must cover every combination: a generic (const auto &, const auto &) arm compiles happily and swallows the cases you forgot.
Two variants instantiate N x M call sites: code size and compile time scale with the product of the alternatives.
std::variant stores the active alternative inline, so one rarely used large alternative inflates every value.

variants.name: Classic accept/visit pair (two virtual calls)
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical form: Element declares accept(Visitor&), every concrete element implements it as v.visit(*this), and overload resolution on the static type of *this selects the visit overload, whose call is virtual again so the operation's runtime type is resolved too. It stays open to new element types and closed to new operations, which is the opposite trade from std::visit. The one-line accept bodies are load-bearing duplication: hoisting them into the base class would pass a Shape& and silently select a fallback overload.
pitfalls: An overload taking the base type (visit(const Shape&)) re-introduces silent fallbacks and destroys the compile-time coverage.
Visitors that accumulate into a member are single-use: a second traversal returns stale state.
Forgetting the virtual destructor on the visitor base leaks or invokes undefined behaviour when visitors are deleted through the base pointer.

variants.name: Type-indexed handler registry (open registration)
variants.implementation_notes: Dispatch through data instead of code: a registry keyed by the std::type_index pair holds handlers as std::function, so a type pair can be registered without touching either class - the right shape for plugins, tests and adapters around foreign hierarchies. The first dispatch is the lookup itself, and the handler downcasts with static_cast only where the key already proves the dynamic type. Choose it when the pair set opens at runtime and a compile-time matrix is not required; prefer std::variant when the set is closed.
pitfalls: typeid on a reference to a non-polymorphic class yields the static type, so the key is silently wrong without at least one virtual function.
The registry outlives the objects that registered handlers: dynamic registration without unregistration is a leak.
The compiler can no longer see the missing cells, so the lookup failure must throw or log - never fall through silently.
